**Solution 1 (answer $t-1$): REJECT.** For $t=2$ the claimed minimum is $1$. A graph with $\rho(G)=1$ has only $K_2$ and $K_1$ components, so it contains no $P_4$. Adding one edge can create at most one $P_4$, so no such graph has two disjoint $P_4$'s after an edge is added. Hence no $2P_4$-saturated graph has spectral radius $1$. The answer $t-1$ is also too small in general, since a saturated graph must contain $t-1$ disjoint $P_4$'s.

**Solution 2 (answer $n-3t+2$): REJECT.** The construction $K_{3(t-1)}\cup K_{n-3(t-1)}$ is not $tP_4$-free for large $n$. For $t=2$, $n=11$, the graph $K_3\cup K_8$ contains two disjoint $P_4$'s inside $K_8$. A valid example shows the formula is not the minimum. Take $K_3\vee\overline{K_8}$ with $n=11$, $t=2$. Every $P_4$ uses at least 2 vertices of $K_3$, so the graph is $2P_4$-free. Adding an edge $v_av_b$ inside the independent set gives $v_c-u_1-v_a-v_b$ and $v_d-u_2-v_e-u_3$, so the graph is saturated. Its spectral radius is $1+\sqrt{1+3\cdot 8}=6<7=n-3t+2$.

**Solution 3 (answer $(t-1)+\sqrt{(t-1)^2+(2t-1)(n-2t+1)}$): REJECT.** The join $K_{2t-1}\vee\overline{K_{n-2t+1}}$ is a valid $tP_4$-saturated graph, but it is not extremal. For $t=2$, $n=8$, consider $K_5\cup K_3$:
- It is $2P_4$-free. Two disjoint $P_4$'s would cover all 8 vertices, so each would lie in one component, but $K_3$ contains no $P_4$.
- It is saturated. For $u\in K_5$ and $w\in K_3$, adding $uw$ gives the disjoint paths $u-w-p-q$ and $a-b-c-d$, where $a,b,c,d\in K_5\setminus\{u\}$ and $p,q$ are the other two vertices of $K_3$.
- Its spectral radius is $\rho(K_5)=4<5$, the value Solution 3 gives for $n=8$, $t=2$.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
